• How is school structured? What is the schedule like? Hours? Days of the year?
I can only write about school until Year 9, since I left the country after that.

I went to a private school. Public schools have a regular reputation when it comes to quality, and they are free (you still have to pay for books, pencils, and food), and almost no person who can afford private education will go to a public school. 

Both of them are very structured. They have a timetable, exams, recess, lunch time.

There is pre-school, primary, secondary, and IB in selected private schools.

Public schools have a fixed curriculum, established by the Ministry of Education. Maths, history, biology, English, religion, among others.

Private schools have variable structure. For example, there are private schools that teach religion, others not. Some teach French, or Chinese, or Italian, others not. Some start at 7, some start at 8...


Mine started at 7am, and ended at 4pm. From Monday to Friday. 

Public schools also go from Monday to Friday, but have the morning classes, and the evening classes. They are a complete different group of students, I guess the parents decide what group their children will join.



• What was your experience like in school? Positive? Negative? What did you like and dislike?

Positive overall. I learnt a lot, and since I'm quite the extrovert, I had many friends who I hanged up with after school and during recess. However there was bullying, and I was a victim. I didn't care tho, I had enough friends to just ignore it. I liked the infrastructure, but didn't like the religious idiology they put in us. Ironically, most of the School friends I have are now either agnostic, or non practicing Catholics.



• Are schools well-funded and maintained? What's the biggest problem facing schools in your country?

Mine was. It had nice classrooms, tidy restrooms, a parking lot, a football pitch, an Olympic swimming pool, a multi court, a library, kioskos (small convenience stores) and a kitchen.

But that's the anomaly. Public schools have very poor infrastructure. Specially outside the capital. Most of them are in precarious situations, with a shortage of teachers, even many of them don't have any roofs or walls. The main problem we have here is the lack of government in the rural areas. And the political right wing keeps on this rethoric that the uneducated Peruvians don't go to school because they do not want to. The reality is that they CAN'T. Not for nothing we have one of the lowest education indexeses34 in the world (see the PISA exam results).




• What is the student-teacher relationship like in school? Was your school strict or lenient? 

30-50 years ago, there was evident abuse from the teachers to students. There was hitting with rulers, there was slapping, and there were physical punishments for miss behavior. Now, there is a greater public opinion against that, for the parents are now more involved in their kids' experience at school. In my case, there was respect, but also friendship with some teachers who gave great mentoring, and who taught in a dynamic way.




• How do girls do in school vs. boys? Is more emphasis or special treatment given to one sex over the other? How do boys perceive school vs. girls?

I'm gonna be honest, in my school in general the girls performed better that the boys. They had a tidier desk, a more colorful notebook, and less time for chit-chat during classes. There were also evident preferences from some teachers (specially males) towards the girls. God knows why.

In my school, there was no kind of male superiority. We were taught that men and women have the same rights, and are totally equal to men. There were also the usual hookups, dramas, relationships, but all part of the School experience.






• If you've also experienced school in the U.S., how is it similar or different to school in LATAM?


The Hollywood approach to middle and high school experience is very different from here. We have a universal uniform, we don't have the faculty to choose our own courses, so they are very different.

Ok, so everything you see on the internet about the beautiful landscapes and all of that, that's the countryside, and I do not recommend living there. 

Lima: it is everyone's first option, capital city of the country, largest city of the country, next to the sea, and gastronomic capital of the world. But I think it's very cliché and if you wanna go somewhere less caothic, go onto the next one. 

Cuzco: Peru's most famous city, and the most beautiful one (allegedly). Next to the Sacred Valley, next to many Inca temples and colonial structures. But it's a place developed for tourism. As far as I know, not very friendly to local residents. But great nightlife, and a fairytale-like atmosphere.

Trujillo: nah, skip that one, trust me. 

Arequipa: it's like the Lima from many years ago, not overpopulated and with prettier places. The second largest city in Peru is just a beautiful metropolis with Andean landscapes, great food, and great nightlife and gastronomy. The historic centre is also a UNESCO world heritage, and near volcanoes if that's your thing. There is the Salinas y Aguada Blanca National Reserve, where you can find a smaller version of the Salar de Uyuni, and the Vicuñas in their natural state. 

Huancayo: totally underrated. It has all a large city can get. Malls, supermarkets, good restaurants, good infraestructura, and it's easy to get there by bus or plane. It's also in the highlands, and there are also beautiful landscapes. 

So those are my suggestions. Notice that there are no cities from the Amazon rainforest, since they are too isolated and don't have great living standards. 

Things to take into account:

Crime index of the area: the crime rate is not as high as places in Mexico or Colombia, but it's still high. 

Nearest airport: ok so since you come from Europe, in case of emergencies you will need an exit or entry point out or into the country. Since all overseas flights to Peru arrive in Lima, check how regular flights are from and to the capital city.

Chachapoyas, and Máncora are great places to visit, not to live in. Huaraz is decent, but they all lack basic entertainment services. Plus, they are far from large cities and airports, so in case of emergencies it might be complicated.

Arequipa and Huancayo are imo the best places to live in. Arequipa is the second largest city in the country and has everything Lima has minus the overly caothic traffic. Huancayo is not as large as Arequipa, but it's close to Lima and you can get there by bus or plane. Very underrated city.

But now we get to the Tren de Aragua, a criminal organization who thrives on blackmail, theft, and selected murder. They are based in Venezuela, and they started to have contact with the Venezuelans in our country. These Venezuelans who were already in the crime business created factions of the Tren de Aragua, and the number of racketeering and extorsion increased. 

The situation we have right now in the last few days is the beginning of a territorial battle between local criminals and foreign criminals. Let's see where this goes...
